newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Merrill inaugurates seat on Argentine bolsa.
newsitem.headline: Merrill inaugurates seat on Argentine bolsa.

text.p: Merrill Lynch inaugurated its incorporation on the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange on Thursday, becoming the first global investment bank to have a seat, president David Komansky said.

"Merrill Lynch has tremendous confidence in Argentina. Argentina is a nation of vibrant opportunity for investors worldwide," Komansky told reporters after executing the first trade from the bank's new seat. According to the bank's local head, Guillermo Reca, trades included buys in YPF, Banco Frances, Banco Galicia and industrial group Perez Companc.
As a sign of confidence in the economy, Winthrop Smith, the president of Merrill Lynch International, said he and Komansky made a couple of personal stock buys as well.

The high-profile arrival of Merrill as a direct participant in the local stock and bond markets was warmly welcomed by the bolsa's president, Julio Macchi. The launch "celebrated a very important act for our markets," he said, adding the presence of a large firm like Merrill is testimony to the local capital market's continued development.
Macchi expected Merrill would be active when derivatives are launched on the exchange in the first quarter of 1997.

Argentina will become the third country in Latin America where Merrill opens a brokerage house, after Brazil and Mexico. The Mexican office was opened at the height of the Tequila crisis last year, something that showed Merrill's commitment to Latin America, the executives said. Merrill has had an office in Buenos Aires for 25 years.

Smith told Reuters "we see our growth opportunities accelerating in Latin America." Although Merrill is only fully represented in Mexico, Brazil and Argentina "essentially our strategy is to be pan-Latin American," he added.

The move reflects Merrill's hopes for the economy. The government's dogged refusal to tinker with the fixed exchange rate pegging the peso to the dollar in the face of the Tequila crisis "has encouraged investors that the right, sound macroeconomics are going to be followed," Smith said.

"We see evidence that activity is picking up -- we think that growth is going to continue to accelerate to 3.5 percent next year and within a couple of years can come back to five percent, or plus with low inflation, which is going to be very positive for the long-term."
Smith said U.S. rates, often considered one of the largest influences on Latin American markets, should remain at "benign levels in 1997, which should bode well for these markets."
"I don't see any 'Tequilas' out there on the horizon, but obviously these are emerging markets so you do have to be cognizant that there is more volatilility than in other markets."

One of the biggest needs for Latin America, though, is higher domestic savings rates. That can make the continent much less dependent on foreign capital and less sensitive to U.S. interest rate changes, Smith said.

Asked if former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo's accusations of corruption in government was a serious problem, Smith replied: "I think corruption is an issue worldwide. Many governments are addressing it. If people perceive it is not being addressed, it is a negative.
"In general, governments need to address it and if they do that will be positive for capital flows."
